narration: Your 401k match is costing you $94,000. I know — everyone says grab the match, it's free money. They're half right. The match is free. The account you're putting it in is the problem. Here's the math. If you make $80,000 and contribute 6% to a traditional 401k for 35 years at 8%, you retire with about $1.4 million. But every dollar comes out taxed as ordinary income. At a realistic 22% effective rate in retirement, you lose roughly $308,000 to the IRS. Now run the same numbers in a Roth 401k — same match, same growth, zero tax on the back end. The difference, after taxes, is about $94,000 in your pocket. Most people default into traditional because HR set it that way in 2009 and nobody updated it. Twenty seconds in your benefits portal flips the switch. The match still hits. The growth still compounds. The IRS just doesn't get a cut at the worst possible time — when you actually need the money. So which one are you in right now — traditional or Roth? Drop it in the comments. And if this reframed how you see your 401k, subscribe. We do this every day.
title: Your 401k Match Is Costing You $94,000
description:
The 401k match isn't the problem — the account type is. Here's the $94,000 math most people never run, and the 20-second fix inside your benefits portal. Traditional or Roth — which one are you in?

narration: Backdoor Roth versus Mega Backdoor Roth — most people don't even know the second one exists. Backdoor Roth: you put $7,000 of after-tax money in, convert it, done. Tax-free forever. narration: Financing a $45,000 car at 7% for 72 months costs you $48,000. Not in payments — in lost wealth. Stay with me. The monthly payment looks fine — about $767. Affordable, right? Over six years you'll pay $55,200 for a car that depreciates to $18,000. You lost $37,000 to depreciation, plus $10,000 in interest. But that's just the visible damage. Now imagine investing that $767 a month at 8% instead. Six years later: $71,000. Twenty years later, untouched: $293,000. The car wasn't a $45,000 decision. It was a $48,000 wealth subtraction — minimum. Here's what rich people actually do. They buy two-to-four-year-old vehicles in cash. Same reliability. Half the price. Zero interest. The depreciation cliff already fell on someone else. The math doesn't care about your favorite brand or how the seats feel. It just compounds, year after year, against the financed car payment. So — financing your next car, or paying cash for used? Comments. Subscribe for more numbers nobody runs.
title: Financing a Car at 7% Costs You $48,000
